## Overview

This is deliberately a step *before* the vascular -> astrocyte -> microglia relay idea, not the relay test itself. Bivariate Moran's I asks a simpler, more basic question first: for a given ligand-receptor pair, does high ligand expression at one location predict high receptor expression nearby, more than tissue-wide spatial autocorrelation alone would predict? That only needs expression + coordinates -- it doesn't need cell-type identity at all, which conveniently sidesteps `10`'s still-unresolved cell-type vocabulary crosswalk (STARmap PLUS's `top_level_cell_type` vs. the Jessberger-reference labels `06`-`08` used). Whatever pairs come out significant here are the ones worth actually stratifying by cell type afterward -- this notebook doesn't presuppose which cell types are involved, it lets the spatial pattern suggest it.

This also isn't a new idea for this project: `03`'s `helper_functions.R` already has a comment about exporting individual RCTD-deconvolved Visium slices specifically "for lianaPlus moran's I" -- this notebook is that same analysis, just run on STARmap PLUS's real single-cell coordinates instead of deconvolved Visium spots.

**Single section only.** `starmap_plus_control_seurat_hippocampus_merged.rds` has all 4 STARmap PLUS sections merged into one object -- `time` (`8months`/`13months`) x `replicate` (`replicate_1`/`replicate_2`), the same way `02`'s `merged_obj` holds every Visium slide. A spatial neighbors graph is a property of one physical piece of tissue -- coordinates from different sections aren't spatially related to each other, so building one shared graph across pooled sections would connect cells that were never physically near each other, just because their raw (x, y) values happen to land close together. This notebook now explicitly restricts to **one representative section** (see `pick-one-section` below) and stays that way deliberately: it's the place to develop and sanity-check the method in depth (bandwidth calibration, local scores, cell-type enrichment) on a single slide. `12_STARmapPLUS_BivariateMoransI_AgeComparison.ipynb` is where all 4 sections actually get run -- each with its own independent graph -- and compared across age.

**Language note.** LIANA+'s bivariate spatial metrics (Moran's I, Lee's L, etc.) live in the Python side of the LIANA+ ecosystem (`liana-py`, built on `squidpy`'s spatial neighbors graph) -- there's no equivalent in the R `liana` package. This notebook only does the R half: loading the Seurat object and exporting the pieces Python needs (expression matrix, coordinates, candidate gene pairs). The actual AnnData construction and Moran's I computation happen in a separate Jupyter notebook, `11b_STARmapPLUS_BivariateMoransI_python.ipynb`, run with the `lianaPlus` conda environment as its kernel.

Originally this mixed R and Python in one document via `reticulate`, but that surfaced a string of low-level C-library conflicts (`typing_extensions`/`torch` version shadowing from `~/.local` user-site packages, then a CUDA-enabled `torch` build failing to preload, then an ABI mismatch between `llvmlite`'s compiled library and the `libstdc++` reticulate's embedded Python picked up) that don't happen when Python runs as its own standalone process. Splitting the two languages into separate files/processes is simpler than fighting reticulate's shared-process quirks: run this notebook's R chunks to export the data, then run `11b` in Jupyter.

```{r setup-r}
#| label: setup-r
library(Seurat)
library(Matrix)

out_dir  <- "starmap_plus_processed"
hpc_path <- file.path(out_dir, "starmap_plus_control_seurat_hippocampus_merged.rds")
```

## Load the hippocampus object and normalize (R)

Moran's I on raw counts would mostly reflect per-cell sequencing depth differences, not real spatial biology, so this log-normalizes first (`Seurat::NormalizeData`, not `SCTransform` -- a simple, fast normalization is enough for a first-pass spatial screen; revisit if results look driven by depth artifacts).

```{r load-and-normalize}
#| label: load-and-normalize

starmap_hpc <- readRDS(hpc_path)
starmap_hpc <- NormalizeData(starmap_hpc, verbose = FALSE)

cat("starmap_hpc:", nrow(starmap_hpc), "genes x", ncol(starmap_hpc), "cells\n")
```

## Restrict to a single section (R)

`NormalizeData` above is a per-cell operation (each cell's own total counts), so it's unaffected by pooling sections -- but the spatial neighbors graph `11b` builds is not, and needs exactly one section's cells. There's no single "sample" column here: a section is identified by the combination of `time` (`8months`/`13months`) and `replicate` (`replicate_1`/`replicate_2`), 2 x 2 = 4 sections total. This builds a combined `section_id` column and subsets down to one section before anything spatial happens downstream.

```{r inspect-sections}
#| label: inspect-sections

# ---- EDIT if these aren't the right column names in your object ----
time_col       <- "time"
replicate_col  <- "replicate"

missing_cols <- setdiff(c(time_col, replicate_col), colnames(starmap_hpc@meta.data))
if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
  cat("Missing expected column(s):", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("Columns present:\n")
  print(colnames(starmap_hpc@meta.data))
  stop("Set time_col/replicate_col above to the columns that actually identify age and replicate.")
}

starmap_hpc$section_id <- paste(starmap_hpc@meta.data[[time_col]], starmap_hpc@meta.data[[replicate_col]], sep = "_")

print(table(starmap_hpc@meta.data[[time_col]], starmap_hpc@meta.data[[replicate_col]]))
```

```{r pick-one-section}
#| label: pick-one-section

# ---- EDIT: pick one section from the table printed above (this just takes the first alphabetically) ----
single_section <- sort(unique(starmap_hpc$section_id))[1]
cat("Restricting to section:", single_section, "\n")

starmap_hpc <- subset(starmap_hpc, subset = section_id == single_section)
cat("starmap_hpc (single section):", nrow(starmap_hpc), "genes x", ncol(starmap_hpc), "cells\n")
```

## Export expression, coordinates, and candidate LR pairs for Python (R)

Manual export (matrix + plain CSVs) rather than an automated Seurat-to-AnnData converter (`SeuratDisk`, `zellkonverter`) -- those are convenient when they work, but their compatibility with a given Seurat/Python/anndata version combination isn't guaranteed, and a hand-built AnnData from plain files is easier to debug if something doesn't line up. `starmap_hpc` at this point is already restricted to the single section chosen above.

```{r export-for-python}
#| label: export-for-python

export_dir <- file.path(out_dir, "starmap_hpc_export")
dir.create(export_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

norm_expr <- GetAssayData(starmap_hpc, layer = "data")  # log-normalized, genes (rows) x cells (cols), single section only

Matrix::writeMM(norm_expr, file.path(export_dir, "expr_norm.mtx"))
writeLines(rownames(norm_expr), file.path(export_dir, "genes.txt"))
writeLines(colnames(norm_expr), file.path(export_dir, "cells.txt"))

coords <- as.data.frame(Embeddings(starmap_hpc, "spatial"))
coords$cell_id <- rownames(coords)
write.csv(coords, file.path(export_dir, "coordinates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

meta <- starmap_hpc@meta.data
meta$cell_id <- rownames(meta)
write.csv(meta, file.path(export_dir, "metadata.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# Candidate LR pairs: the full sig_pairs_present set from 10, not pre-filtered to any
# assumed cell-type pair -- this run is a global, unbiased screen across the whole
# hippocampus, not restricted to vascular/astrocyte/microglia specifically (yet).
sig_pairs_present <- read.csv(file.path(out_dir, "sig_pairs_present_starmap.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
lr_pairs_export <- unique(sig_pairs_present[, c("ligand_complex", "receptor_complex")])
write.csv(lr_pairs_export, file.path(export_dir, "lr_pairs.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

cat("Exported to:", export_dir, "\n")
cat("Candidate LR pairs for the Moran's I screen:", nrow(lr_pairs_export), "\n")
```

## Continue in Jupyter

Open `11b_STARmapPLUS_BivariateMoransI_python.ipynb` (same directory), select the `lianaPlus` kernel, and run it top to bottom -- it reads directly from `export_dir` above. It builds the AnnData object, the squidpy spatial neighbors graph, checks the installed `liana-py`'s `bivariate()` signature before calling it, runs the Moran's I screen across `lr_pairs.csv`, and saves the resulting AnnData (with whatever liana-py adds to `obsm`/`uns`) back to `starmap_hpc_bivariate_morans.h5ad` in the same export folder.

## Notes on interpretation

This screen deliberately runs on the whole hippocampus at once, not stratified by cell type -- a significant global Moran's I for a pair says the ligand and receptor spatially co-vary somewhere in the tissue, not which cell types are driving it. The natural next step for any pair that comes out significant is to look at *local* Moran's I / LISA scores per cell (wherever liana-py exposes them -- check `11b`'s results cell) and overlay `celltype_merged` (from `10`) on the cells with the highest local scores, to see empirically which cell types are actually co-located there. That's what should inform whether a specific pair really looks like a vascular -> astrocyte or astrocyte -> microglia signal, rather than assuming the cell types up front.
